title: The dynamics of e^(πi)
question: Following the motion of e^(it) around the unit circle, where does e^(πi) land?
explanation: e^(it) moves around the unit circle at unit speed; after time π it has gone half way around, landing on -1.

title: 100 random chords, how many intersections?
question: On average, how many intersections do 100 random chords of a circle have?
explanation: There are 100·99/2 = 4950 pairs of chords and two random chords cross with probability 1/3, so the expected count is 4950/3 = 1650.
comment: answer derived mathematically; review against video

title: The ladybug clock puzzle
question: A ladybug starts at 12 on a clock and randomly steps to a neighbouring number until it has visited every number. What is the probability that 6 is the last number visited?
explanation: Surprisingly, each of the 11 numbers other than 12 is equally likely to be last, so the probability is 1/11.

title: How Earth's size was computed by Eratosthenes
question: What did Eratosthenes compare to compute the size of the Earth?
options: The shape of Earth's shadow during a lunar eclipse
The angle of the Sun's shadows at noon in two cities a known distance apart
How long a ship took to sail around Africa
The height of mountains seen from the sea
explanation: The Sun's rays hit Syene and Alexandria at different angles; that angle difference, plus the distance between the cities, gives Earth's circumference.

title: How Aristarchus deduced the distance to the moon
question: What did Aristarchus use to deduce the distance to the Moon?
options: Radar echoes bounced off the Moon
The size of Earth's shadow on the Moon during a lunar eclipse
explanation: By comparing the size of Earth's shadow on the Moon during a lunar eclipse to the Moon itself, Aristarchus related the Moon's size and distance to Earth's size.

title: The Parker Square
question: What is the Parker Square?
options: A proof that every number is a sum of four squares
An attempt at a 3x3 magic square made of square numbers that doesn't quite work
A tiling of the plane using squares of different sizes
A square whose side length is irrational
explanation: Matt Parker's 3x3 grid of square numbers has rows and columns with equal sums, but one diagonal fails, so it is not a true magic square of squares.

title: Pizza proof 0.999... = 1
question: What does the video show that 0.999... (nines repeating forever) equals?
explanation: One third is 0.333..., and three thirds of a pizza make the whole pizza, so 0.999... = 3 × 0.333... = 1.

title: What does sine actually mean?
question: For a right triangle with angle θ, what is sin(θ)?
options: Opposite side divided by adjacent side
explanation: Sine is the ratio opposite/hypotenuse; on a unit circle it is the height (y-coordinate) of the point at angle θ.

title: Butterfly method for fractions
question: Using the butterfly method, what is 1/2 + 1/3?
explanation: Cross-multiply for the numerator (1×3 + 2×1 = 5) and multiply the denominators (2×3 = 6): 5/6.

title: Secret reason it's called pizza
question: A pizza has radius z and thickness a. What is its volume?
explanation: A pizza is a cylinder: volume = π·r²·h = pi·z·z·a, which spells 'pizza'.

title: Hardest multiple choice question ever
question: In the self-referential question 'If you choose an answer to this question at random, what is the chance you will be correct?' with options 25%, 50%, 60%, 25%, why is 25% not a consistent answer?
options: Because two options say 25%, so picking 25% at random has a 50% chance
Because there are only three options
explanation: Two of the four options are 25%, so randomly picking 25% happens half the time, contradicting the 25% claim. Every answer leads to a contradiction.

title: Coin Tosses, HTT vs TTH
question: Flipping a fair coin repeatedly, which pattern is more likely to appear first: HTT or TTH?
explanation: TTH only wins if the first two flips are TT (probability 1/4). Once any H appears first, the first TT that follows completes HTT, so HTT wins 3/4 of the time.

title: Ramanujan Nested Radicals
question: What does Ramanujan's nested radical √(1 + 2√(1 + 3√(1 + 4√(1 + ...)))) equal?
explanation: Using n = √(1 + (n-1)(n+1)) repeatedly starting from n = 3, the infinite nested radical equals 3.

title: How An Infinite Hotel Ran Out Of Room
question: Hilbert's infinite hotel is full. How can it still fit one new guest?
options: It can't; a full hotel is full
Every guest moves from room n to room n+1, freeing room 1
explanation: Shifting each guest up one room frees room 1 while everyone still has a room. The hotel only 'runs out of room' for uncountably many new guests.

title: It's impossible to choose a number at random
question: Why can't you choose a positive whole number uniformly at random?
options: Computers can't generate big enough numbers
Equal probabilities for infinitely many numbers can't add up to exactly 1
Only odd numbers can be chosen randomly
Because there is a largest whole number
explanation: If each number had the same probability p, the total would be 0 when p = 0 or infinite when p > 0, never 1.

title: Incomplete open cubes
question: How many distinct 'incomplete open cubes' did artist Sol LeWitt catalogue?
explanation: LeWitt's work shows the 122 distinct ways to remove edges from a cube frame so that what remains is still a connected 3D form (counting rotations as the same).

title: Measuring the entropy of English
question: What does measuring the entropy of English estimate?
options: How many words are in the dictionary
The average number of bits of information each letter carries, given how predictable text is
The number of letters in the alphabet
explanation: Entropy measures average surprise; because English is predictable, each letter carries far fewer than log2(26) ≈ 4.7 bits.

title: Measuring the speed of light using Jupiter's moons
question: How did Jupiter's moons reveal that light has a finite speed?
options: The moons looked bluer when closer to Earth
The timing of Io's eclipses shifted depending on how far Earth was from Jupiter
The moons cast shadows on Earth
Jupiter's moons orbit at the speed of light
explanation: When Earth was farther from Jupiter, Io's eclipses appeared later, because light needed extra time to cross the extra distance.

title: Why the ancient Greeks rejected heliocentrism
question: A key reason the ancient Greeks rejected a Sun-centred model is that they observed no...
options: Stellar parallax: shift in the stars' positions over a year
explanation: If Earth orbited the Sun, nearby stars should shift over a year. The stars are so far away that this parallax was too small for them to see.

title: How to measure nearby galaxies
question: Which 'standard candle' lets astronomers measure the distance to nearby galaxies?
options: Cepheid variable stars, whose pulsation period reveals their true brightness
explanation: Henrietta Leavitt found that a Cepheid's pulsation period tells you its true brightness; comparing that to its apparent brightness gives its distance.

title: When you lose weight where does it go?
question: When you lose fat, where does most of the mass go?
options: It is converted into pure energy
You breathe it out as carbon dioxide
explanation: Fat is broken down into carbon dioxide and water; most of the mass leaves your body as CO2 that you exhale.

title: Why do these metronomes sync up?
question: Why do metronomes on a shared movable platform end up in sync?
options: The movable platform passes tiny pushes between them, coupling their motion
Gravity from each metronome pulls the others
explanation: Each swing nudges the shared base, which nudges the other metronomes; this coupling gradually pulls them into phase.

title: How does light 'know' the shortest path?
question: What principle says light travels along the path that takes the least time?
explanation: Fermat's principle of least time explains reflection and refraction; quantum mechanics explains it as nearby paths reinforcing while others cancel.

title: The tragic tale of Guillaume Le Gentil
question: Guillaume Le Gentil travelled to India to observe which rare event, and kept missing it?
options: The transit of Venus across the Sun
explanation: Le Gentil set out to observe the 1761 transit of Venus, missed it at sea, waited eight years for the 1769 transit, and was clouded out.
